title: Java in practice
lead: Which Java techniques made this project fast, and by how much? Plain numeric Java, the Vector API, TornadoVM on the GPU, virtual threads, TeaVM in the browser, and Hilla for the online mode. Every number comes from a measurement in the repository, with its limits.
toc.outlook: Valhalla and the final Vector API
sec.overview.title: Java in this project
sec.overview.p1: The project is a Java demo first. The same game logic runs on the JVM, on a GPU through {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM}, and in the browser through {term:teavm|TeaVM}. This page walks through the techniques, each with a snippet cut from the repository and the measured effect.
sec.overview.p2: The chart compares one forward pass of the SMALL network. The three Mac rows come from one run. The other rows come from other machines and other runs, so compare them by order of magnitude only.
sec.plain-java.title: Fast plain Java
sec.plain-java.p1: The search code avoids objects. A move is one `int`. The board is a `byte[]` with one entry per cell. The search plays a move with make and unmake on one mutable position instead of copying it, and the undo data lives in parallel primitive arrays.
sec.plain-java.p2: Move generation writes into a buffer that the caller owns and returns a count. The jump search keeps its visited set of 121 cells in two `long` values, so no set object is allocated. Incremental evaluation made the search about 1.3 times faster in nodes per second.
sec.plain-java.p3: Against a faithful C++ port, the Java search reaches about 1.6 million nodes per second on one Apple M3 Max core. The hardened C++ build is 1.5 to 1.7 times as fast. Java starts slower: 0.85 s against 0.26 s to the end of a one-position search.
sec.vector-api.title: Vector API
sec.vector-api.p1: The network on the CPU uses the {term:vector-api|Vector API}. The inner loop of the convolution keeps eight accumulators in vector registers and uses {term:fma|fused multiply-add}. On one M3 Max core this is about 15 times the scalar reference.
sec.vector-api.p2: On an Intel Sapphire Rapids core, AVX-512 reaches about 3 times the AVX2 result. A C++ SIMD port is about 12 % faster on the Mac. The build adds `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`; without the module the server falls back to the scalar network.
sec.auto-vectorization.title: Auto-vectorization
sec.auto-vectorization.p1: This project does not use auto-vectorization and did not measure it. HotSpot can turn simple counted loops over arrays into SIMD instructions on its own. That works only for loop shapes the compiler recognises, and it does not reorder floating-point sums. For the hex convolution the project chose explicit vectors.
sec.tornadovm.title: TornadoVM
sec.tornadovm.p1: {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} compiles Java {term:kernel|kernels} to Metal or CUDA. The first snippet is the naive hex convolution: the two outer loops become the GPU grid. The second shows a {term:task-graph|task graph}: weights are copied once, inputs on every call.
sec.tornadovm.p2: At batch 256 on the M3 Max the GPU is about 37 times one Vector API thread. At batch 1 it does not pay. On a Tesla T4, TornadoVM and hand-written CUDA reach the same throughput, about 85,000 SMALL evaluations per second.
sec.tornadovm.p3: The limits: a cold start of 3 to 4 seconds against about 0.2 s for C++ CUDA, no bounds checks on the device, device math that differs from Java, and a new compilation for each new batch size.
sec.outlook.title: Valhalla and the final Vector API
sec.outlook.p1: Status checked on 2026-11-21. JEP 401 (value objects, preview) is targeted to JDK 28. The Vector API is in its twelfth incubation (JEP 537, JDK 27) and will incubate until the features of Project Valhalla are available as preview. The project compiles with `--release 25`, so none of this is in use.
sec.outlook.p2: The block below is an illustration. It is not in the repository, not compiled and not measured. It shows how a move could become a type instead of a packed `int`.
sec.more.title: Also in the code
sec.more.p1: {term:virtual-thread|Virtual threads} feed the GPU: hundreds of games park while one {term:device-thread|device thread} collects their positions. A first version with a semaphore over platform threads reached 29,000 to 46,000 evaluations per second; virtual threads reached 57,000 to 82,000.
sec.more.p2: TeaVM compiles the Java search to WebAssembly GC for the browser: 0.69 times the speed of the JVM, about half of the C++ WebAssembly build. The network forward pass stays in C++. TornadoVM copies between heap and device with the {term:ffm-api|Foreign Function & Memory API}.
sec.hilla.title: Java and React without REST
sec.hilla.p1: In the online mode one Java class, annotated {term:browser-callable|@BrowserCallable}, is the whole server API. {term:hilla|Hilla} generates a TypeScript client for it, and the shared React code calls it like a local function.
sec.hilla.p2: On the wire each call is a POST to `/connect/GameEndpoint/<method>` with a JSON body and a {term:csrf-token|CSRF token}. The offline build drops the Hilla branch at build time, and the build script checks that no file contains `connect/`.
